implementation_notes: Python has no private state to protect and no value assignment semantics, so a memento is an explicit copy: copy.deepcopy for arbitrary object graphs (cycle-safe through its memo and customisable via __deepcopy__) or a frozen dataclass with copy.replace (dataclasses.replace before 3.13) for value-style states. The caretaker is a list or a collections.deque(maxlen=N) whose bound silently discards the oldest entries, and undo is an assignment of the stored value. Because a frozen dataclass is immutable and hashable it can be shared without further copying, while a mutable snapshot must be copied again if the originator keeps holding it. A classic Memento class remains justified when the snapshot must carry behaviour, such as restoring itself into the originator.
pitfalls: Shallow copies share nested containers (copy.copy, list[:], dict.copy), so a 'snapshot' taken that way changes with the original; deepcopy is the default answer for nested state.

deepcopy copies too much as readily as too little: shared collaborators and caches are duplicated unless __deepcopy__ is implemented, and objects like modules, sockets and file handles are not copied at all.
deque(maxlen=N) silently discards the oldest memento, which is the desired bound but must be an explicit decision rather than a surprise in the undo UI.
Attributes that must not be captured (locks, connections, log handles) need __getstate__/__setstate__ or __deepcopy__ control; otherwise snapshots fail or duplicate resources.

variants.name: Pickled state mementos for durable history
variants.implementation_notes: When snapshots must outlive the process or be shipped, pickle the originator's state: pickle.dumps/loads convert object graphs to bytes (protocol 5 is available from 3.8 and the default from 3.14), and __getstate__/__setstate__ define exactly which attributes constitute the state, which is also how non-copyable resources are kept out of snapshots. The caretaker stores bytes in a deque or on disk, and restore unpickles and feeds the state back through the originator. Use it for durability rather than hot in-memory undo: it is slower than deepcopy, and binding snapshots to a class definition turns every schema change into a versioning task.
pitfalls: pickle is not secure: unpickling untrusted bytes executes arbitrary code, and the documentation states plainly that it must never be fed data from an untrusted source - history must come from your own storage.
A pickle is bound to the class definition and its import path, so renaming or moving the class breaks stored snapshots; persist a plain dict or DTO when the schema churns.
Objects that cannot be pickled (open files, sockets, lambdas, local classes, locks) must be excluded via __getstate__ and rebuilt by the originator on restore.
